subject: Clarify SLA: streaming vs sync endpoint commitments
messages:
From: Bethany Rogers <bethany.rogers@astralhealth.com>
To: Marcus Lin <marcus.lin@redwood.com>
Cc: Tom Delgado <tom.delgado@astralhealth.com>
Date: Mon, 12 Oct 2026 09:15:00 -0700
Subject: SLA ask: streaming behavior and rate guarantees

Marcus — thanks for the demo last week. We like Redwood's dedicated offering but we need to lock ASA/SLA language around streaming endpoints before procurement can finalize. Two quick asks from our infra and compliance teams: 

1) Time-to-first-token (TTFT) definition — do you guarantee TTFT on streaming endpoints or only on non-streaming (sync) completion times? Our use case hinges on interactive experiences where users must see the first token within X ms.

2) Sustained tokens/sec expectations — we plan to burst at short intervals but sustain 250 tokens/sec average per session for inference-heavy workflows. Can you confirm whether streaming endpoints are covered by the same tokens/sec SLOs as non-streaming endpoints, or if there are carve-outs?

We attached our draft SLA excerpt and a simple traffic matrix. If you can propose explicit wording (or an exception carve-out) we can move forward with procurement.

Thanks — Bethany

Bethany — really appreciate the clear asks and the attachment. Looping in Neha (legal) and Lauren (serving/runtime). High level: we treat streaming endpoints differently in practice because TTFT is a distinct metric from end-to-end completion latency, and sustained token-rate guarantees depend on whether requests are routed through burst pools vs. dedicated pools.

Request: can you share a couple of target TTFT numbers (p99 preferred) and the expected concurrency per session? That will help Lauren map to our serving profiles and propose a carve-out if necessary.

I'll follow up with concrete suggested SLA language once we confirm targets.

Bethany / Marcus — quick legal framing from our side so you can see what we typically commit to: 

- We define TTFT as the time from accepted request to first byte/token emitted to the client at p99. For streaming endpoints we have historically published TTFT targets tied to dedicated pools (e.g., 150ms p99) while for multi-tenant hosted pools we provide best-effort TTFTs and rely on fallbacks.
- Sustained tokens/sec SLOs are scoped per routed pool. If a customer opts for a Dedicated capacity commitment we can include a tokens/sec SLO for both streaming and non-streaming endpoints in the contract; otherwise, streaming endpoints on shared pools are excluded from hard tokens/sec guarantees (we provide throughput guidance and throttling policies).

If Astral needs the streaming endpoints covered under the same hard SLOs without Dedicated capacity, we will need an exception, an uplifted price tier, or an explicit traffic-shaping/ingress policy agreed for bursts. Marcus — do you have precedent language for an exception and the associated pricing delta?

Neha

Hi all — quick technical note based on Astral's numbers (you said ~250 tokens/sec sustained per session and occasional bursts to 1k tokens/sec):

- Streaming TTFT: On Dedicated pools we can hit ~120–180ms p99 for short prompt lengths (<=64 tokens). For longer prefix lengths p99 rises due to KV cache warm-up; we recommend explicit prefix caching for chat-style workflows.
- Sustained tokens/sec: 250 tokens/sec sustained across many concurrent streams requires capacity reservations per session — otherwise the platform will multiplex and you should expect per-stream effective rates to vary. 
- Recommended contract carve-out: if you want hard tokens/sec guarantees for streaming without Dedicated capacity, we can define a "Streaming Rate Exception" that:
  * Limits the guaranteed window to steady-state sessions only (post-auth/warm-up),
  * Caps guaranteed burst duration (e.g., 30s bursts at up to 1k tokens/sec), and
  * Ties exceptions to an ingress shaping rule and a reserve buffer (extra X GPUs or reserved tokens).

I attached a short matrix showing expected p50/p90/p99 for TTFT and tokens/sec across different pool types. Happy to walk through it on a call.

Thanks — Lauren

Bethany — thanks for the numbers. Based on Astral's targets and our internal guidance, here is a proposed carve-out we can include in the contract (draft language below). If this looks acceptable I will have Legal put it into the next SLA revision and Procurement can proceed.

--- Proposed clause (draft) ---
Streaming Endpoint Carve-out: For the purposes of this Agreement, Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) shall be defined as the elapsed time between Redwood’s acceptance of a request and the emission of the first token to the client. For Dedicated Capacity customers, Redwood warrants a TTFT not to exceed 200ms at p99 for streaming endpoints for prompt prefixes up to 128 tokens. For non-Dedicated (shared) pools, TTFT is provided on a best-effort basis and is not an express contractual SLO.

Token Throughput Guarantees: Redwood will guarantee sustained token throughput only for endpoints served from Dedicated capacity where a committed tokens/sec reservation is purchased. For Astral Health (Deal AST-2026-004), Redwood will provide a Streaming Rate Exception that guarantees:
  • Sustained per-session throughput of 250 tokens/sec (average) for sessions enrolled in the reserved pool,
  • Burst allowance up to 1,000 tokens/sec for a continuous window not to exceed 30 seconds per burst,
  • Ingress shaping and session registration are required for the Exception; Redwood may throttle or reroute non-registered traffic.

Pricing/Offset: The Exception will be tied to an uplifted reserve commitment (detailed in the attached pricing exhibit). Coverage will be limited to traffic routed to the reserved pool and will be subject to standard outage/fallback provisions.

If Astral is aligned we can convert this into formal contract language and include references to monitoring and SLO reporting dashboards (we will provide p50/p90/p99 dashboards and monthly tokens/sec reports).

Best — Marcus
